newsitem.title: BELGIUM: COREPER fails to reach deal on shipbuilding aid.
newsitem.headline: COREPER fails to reach deal on shipbuilding aid.

text.p: COREPER failed to reach a compromise on Wednesday on a proposal to extend EU rules allowing shipbuilding aid in the absence of an international deal to scrap most support to the sector, EU sources said on Thursday.
However, diplomats will continue their efforts next week in an effort to avoid holding an extraordinary Industry Council that has been tentatively scheduled for September 20.
The issue is a problem because the United States has so far not ratified an accord brokered in 1994 by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development.
The EU is now struggling with whether and for how long to extend its 7th shipbuilding directive, 90/684/EEC, which allows aid of up to nine percent of contract value.
The Council decided last year that current aid rules would apply in the absence of the OECD deal, but only until October 1, which is why the EU now has to take a new decision.
In July, the Commission proposed legislation COM(96)309 to enable the EU to extend the directive until the end of 1998 or the entry into force of the international agreement.
However, some member states believe that is too long while Sweden, Finland, Denmark and the Netherlands would like the EU to scrap its aid now, even without ratification of the OECD deal.
A majority of countries at the meeting of COREPER, the EU Committee of Permanent Representatives, supported extending the aid but differed over what deadline to set, the sources said.
Germany and Britain preferred 1997 while France, Greece and Spain supported the Commission's proposal, an EU diplomat said.
Officials stress that as soon as the OECD accord takes force, the EU rules would lapse automatically.

The Irish presidency also raised the possibility on Wednesday of ending support in cases where EU shipyards faced no international competition. But delegations need to consult their capitals because that is a new concept, an EU source said.
The OECD agreement would eliminate all direct shipbuilding subsidies except social aid and, within certain ceilings, aid for research and development.
But the deal, which was originally due to take force in January, faces ratification problems in the United States.

The Republican-controlled House of Representatives endorsed it on June 13, but adopted amendments that would delay key sections by 30 months, leading the Clinton administration to warn the agreement might not be ratified.
U.S. shipyards argue they have not had enough time to adjust to the commercial era after the loss of military contracts at the end of the Cold War.
The EU, which represents about 20 percent of the world shipbuilding market, ratified the OECD agreement in December, saying it would help improve market access for its shipyards.
